definition: An iterative cycle where an AI model reasons, selects a tool, observes the outcome, and repeats until the goal is met.
A central agent that breaks down a complex user query into sub-tasks and delegates them to specialized sub-agents.
A decentralized multi-agent pattern where agents coordinate via direct hand-offs rather than a central hub.
The ability of a model to generate structured arguments for predefined external functions/tools.
A design pattern where a human must approve or intervene in an agentic workflow, especially for high-stakes actions.
An architectural pattern where a central agent analyzes the user's intent and routes the query to the most appropriate specialized sub-agent.
An agent responsible for decomposing a complex goal into a sequence of executable sub-tasks.
An agentic pattern where one model generates a draft and another (the evaluator) provides feedback for iterative refinement.
A safety constraint that bounds the number of iterative steps an autonomous agent can take to prevent infinite loops.
The process of breaking a complex, high-level goal into smaller, manageable sub-tasks.
A pattern where tasks are split among parallel agents (Map) and results are combined by an aggregator (Reduce).
The persistence of conversation history and tool outputs across multiple turns in an agentic session.
An agent that classifies user input to select the most appropriate specialized tool or sub-agent.
The specific character or role defined in the system prompt to guide the model's tone and domain behavior.
An internal feedback loop where the model reviews its initial output against constraints and improves it.
A technique where multiple agents cross-examine each other's reasoning to reach a higher-accuracy consensus.
An agent that manages a team of worker agents, deciding which one is best suited for each step in a workflow.
Running non-dependent agentic tasks simultaneously to reduce total wall-clock latency.
The process where an agent searches a tool registry to find the correct API for a specific sub-task.
A centralized architecture where a single hub manages all communication and delegation between worker agents.
An agent that can pursue complex goals over many turns without needing constant user intervention.
A specialized agent with a narrow scope designed to perform one type of labor (e.g., coding, research).
The maximum allowed time for an agentic loop to complete before it's considered a failure for UX purposes.
The conversation history stored in the context window for the current session.
A step where the agent critiques its own work or plan to identify errors before final execution.
Anthropic's open standard for connecting AI models to data sources and tools via a unified interface.
A service that exposes resources, tools, and prompts to an AI client following the MCP specification.
The standard transport protocol for real-time, streaming updates from an MCP server over a network.
The lightweight remote procedure call protocol used for messaging in the MCP specification.
An executable function exposed by an MCP server that the model can call to interact with external systems.
A read-only data source (e.g., a file or database record) exposed by an MCP server for model context.
A local communication method for MCP where clients and servers exchange messages via standard input/output streams.
The phase where an MCP client queries a server to find out which features (tools, resources, etc.) it supports.
A security boundary (e.g., a specific folder) defined in the MCP server configuration to limit file access.
A feature allowing an MCP server to request text generation from the AI model via the client.
The MCP request used by a client to discover all executable functions available on a server.
The MCP request used to discover all available data sources a server can provide to the model.
A pre-defined instruction template provided by a server to guide the model's behavior for a specific task.
The mechanism (Stdio or SSE) that moves JSON-RPC messages between MCP participants.
The unique identifier (e.g., file:// or postgres://) used to locate a specific MCP resource.
The application (e.g., Claude Desktop) that manages the model and connects it to multiple MCP servers.
The handshake process where a client and server agree on protocol versions and exchange capabilities.
Notifications sent from a server to a client to indicate the status of a long-running tool execution.
URIs with placeholders (e.g., file://{path}) that allow a server to expose a dynamic range of resources.
MCP's ability to handle non-text data (like images or PDF bytes) via base64 or optimized stream handling.
The states of a server connection, including initialization, active, and graceful shutdown.
A one-way message in MCP that doesn't require a response, used for status updates or logs.
The design pattern where the model decides when to call MCP tools based on user input.
Using an MCP server as a bridge to translate legacy protocols (SQL, SOAP) into standard MCP tools.
The goal of MCP: a single way for any model to talk to any data source or tool.
The project-level configuration file that defines technical conventions and architectural rules for Claude Code.
Anthropic's agentic CLI tool for coding, capable of refactoring, testing, and navigating codebases.
A command in Claude Code used to perform text-based searches across the project to find specific patterns.
A command used to trigger the execution of unit or integration tests within the project environment.
A configuration file used to hide sensitive or irrelevant directories from Claude Code's view.
A continuous session in Claude Code allowing for back-and-forth chat and agentic command execution.
The ability of an agent like Claude Code to run shell commands to verify code or gather system info.
A command to list files and map out the project structure for the agent.
A utility to reduce conversation history tokens to stay within the model context limit.
The process where Claude Code independently analyzes and modifies code across multiple files.
The command used to set up a project and generate initial CLAUDE.md and .claudeignore files.
Strategic removal of older messages in Claude Code to focus on the current task while staying under token limits.
A setting where Claude Code requires user approval before executing any terminal command.
The internal cognitive loop Claude Code uses to process tool results and plan the next coding step.
Claude Code's ability to stage, commit, and describe code changes directly in the version control system.
A command for the agent to analyze the current codebase for bugs, anti-patterns, or convention violations.
Environment variables or files used to customize the behavior of the Claude Code CLI tool.
The strategy used by agents to build features through small, verified, and tested code changes.
A command (or intent) used to report a failure, triggering the agent to investigate and propose a fix.
Claude Code's capability to use standard Unix utilities (grep, find, sed) to manipulate the codebase.
The project-specific rules (naming, patterns) defined in CLAUDE.md that the agent must strictly follow.
The model's ability to write its own test cases to verify the correctness of the code it just modified.
The system's ability to monitor current context usage and warn the user when limits are approaching.
The set of files the agent can 'see' and modify based on its current working directory and ignore rules.
The high-level concept of using tools like Claude Code as a real-time collaborator in the terminal.
Providing a small number of input-output examples in the prompt to guide model behavior.
Encouraging the model to think step-by-step before answering to improve reasoning accuracy.
Foundational instructions provided at the start of a session to define persona and global rules.
Providing the start of the model's response (e.g., '{') to force specific formatting like JSON.
Structural markers used to provide clear instructions and boundaries in Claude prompts.
A vulnerability where user input tricks the model into ignoring its system-level constraints.
Using an AI model to design or optimize the prompts for other agents in a system.
Explicitly telling the model what NOT to do (e.g., 'Do not include conversational filler').
Internal tokens used by models like Claude 3.7 to explore solutions before final output.
Using tool-use or few-shot patterns to ensure output follows a rigid JSON or XML structure.
Asking the model to perform a task without providing any prior examples in the prompt.
A parameter controlling output randomness (0.0 for deterministic, 1.0 for creative).
Tokens that signal the model to stop generating text, used for delimiting structured blocks.
Assigning a specific identity (e.g., 'Senior Cloud Architect') to influence output quality and tone.
Retrieving task-specific examples from a database to include in the prompt for every query.
A delimited section (e.g., <thought>) where the model's intermediate reasoning is stored.
Providing background info early in the prompt to set the 'mental stage' for the model's task.
Limiting the model's vocabulary or format to a specific set of allowed values or tokens.
When information from one part of a complex prompt unintentionally influences another unrelated part.
Designing prompts to be as concise as possible to save on API costs and latency.
Inputs designed to test the model's safety boundaries and instruction-following limits.
Ordering instructions so the model prioritizes the most critical rules (e.g., placing constraints at the end).
Treating prompts as code and tracking changes to monitor performance drifts over time.
The practice of storing prompts in version control and deploying them via CI/CD pipelines.
The systematic process of refining model inputs to achieve high-quality, reliable outputs.
Storing frequently used context (like system prompts) to reduce latency and API costs.
The maximum amount of information (tokens) a model can process in a single interaction.
The latency between sending a request and receiving the first part of the response.
The process of breaking down text into smaller numerical units (tokens) for the model.
Injecting external data from a database into the model's context to provide updated knowledge.
Breaking large documents into smaller, overlapping segments for precise vector search retrieval.
A numerical representation of text that captures semantic meaning for similarity searching.
Strategic removal of older or irrelevant parts of a conversation to stay within token limits.
When a model retrieves a pre-computed context block from memory, saving time and money.
The phenomenon where LLMs lose information placed in the center of very long prompts.
Adding high-level summaries to document chunks before embedding to preserve semantic meaning.
The total time the model takes to generate a response, dependent on size and token count.
The hard cap on the number of tokens a model can accept or generate in one turn.
Searching based on meaning and intent rather than exact keyword matches.
Using non-semantic tags (like date or category) to narrow down results in a RAG search.
A specialized model used solely to convert text into vector embeddings (e.g., Voyage AI).
Combining keyword-based (BM25) and semantic (vector) search for improved accuracy.
The model's ability to accurately reference specific facts from deep within a large context window.
Using an AI model to summarize or 'zip' long histories before sending them to the primary model.
The practice of repeating text between document segments to prevent semantic cutting in RAG.
When a context block isn't found in cache and must be processed from scratch at full cost.
A parameter limiting the length of the model's generation to prevent runaway token costs.
The time-to-live for a cached context block before it is automatically evicted from memory.
When the topic changes so much that early session context is no longer relevant but still consumes tokens.
The practice of achieving the best model performance with the minimum number of input tokens.
